en: A Hymn on the Auspicious Dawn.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Though he has been praised with hymns of praise by the hosts of gods, by the foremost of Siddhas and Gandharvas, and by distinguished ascetics in heaven and on earth—
I too, though my power is meager, shall praise the Noble One, the Fully Awakened.
When Garuḍa flies through the sky, why do the bees not follow? [1] || 1 ||

O Jina, just as a lotus is fully awakened at the end of the night, so too have you been perfectly awakened in this world through the attainment of instantaneous knowledge, amidst the dense darkness of the night of all-pervading afflictions.
I shall entreat [thee] with devotion by means of these clusters of flowers of praise. ||2||
He who has destroyed the faction of evil, whose defects are entirely exhausted, whose complexion is like molten gold, whose eyes are as long as full-blown lotuses,
who possesses a most beautiful halo, and who is endowed with the splendor of a radiant circle of light.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. [3.2]
To the conqueror of the power of Māra, the destroyer of the Kāpotī cave, the benefactor of the three worlds, the remover of the thicket of the creeper of womanhood,
the knower of the supreme bliss of tranquility, and the breaker of the mountain of ignorance—
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 4 [3]
While the Buddha— the first-born among asuras, suras, and humans, the creator of all worlds, the sole word for the creation of the universe,
whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals— sleeps in the world;
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. [4]
Though standing on the slope of the eastern mountain, copper-red like a slice of coral,
the destroyer of the mass of darkness, and the sole eye of all people, even the sun has now fallen asleep, intoxicated by its own splendor.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you; may your morning be auspicious. [6] (5)
Even that moon, white as the tusk of an elephant, the cool-rayed one who is the tilaka of the night and the crest-jewel of Śiva,
has fallen asleep, its ruddy glow of passion not yet departed.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. [6]
Even that Creator, the lotus-born Brahmā, who possesses four excellent arms, eight faces (four times two),
who knows the rules for recitation and ritual observances, and who is the expounder of the Sāmaveda,
has fallen asleep.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. [8] (7)
Blue as the petal of a water-lily, with eyes as broad as white lotuses, the slayer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods, the creator of the universe and the one whose form is the universe—
Hari himself, though long asleep, remains unreleased from dwelling in the womb.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 9 [10]
Resembling the peak of the snowy mountain, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, skilled in the destruction of the three cities, and clad in an upper garment of tiger skin,
the wielder of the trident sleeps eternally together with the daughter of the foremost of mountains.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 10 [8]
Paśupati, with his mass of matted hair tawny like that of a Kapila cow and eyes as red as copper, is uniquely skilled at destroying unions even at the most inopportune time;
yet even he, his body shattered by the arrows of Smara, has fallen asleep like a sacrificial fire.
O Ten-Powered One, may there be for you always a most auspicious dawn at daybreak. 11 [11]
Though he holds a blazing thunderbolt in his hand and is difficult for the Dānavas to conquer, even the Lord of the Gods has his mind deluded by the amorous charms of Śacī;
day and night he remains asleep, submerged in the mire of passion.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 12 [9]
Resembling snow, the moon, and the white water-lily, with eyes reddened from drinking wine,
his limbs and arms firm and hard, his hand grasping a plow—
Balarāma lies here, long asleep, his neck entwined around Revatī.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak! 13 [12]
The elephant-faced one, the sole possessor of tusks, the creator of obstacles everywhere, with the ichor of rut flowing from him, his temples resonating with the humming of bees—
even Gaṇapati himself sleeps, intoxicated by the drinking of wine.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 14 [13]

Even that Kumāra, the son of the Three-eyed One— the slayer of Krauñca, the six-faced one with a body like fresh gold, whose spear at the tip of his hand is blue as the Atasī flower— he too is asleep.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 15 [14]
Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, the lords of the Yakṣas, Daityas, and Uragas, as well as the other world-protectors dwelling in heaven, on earth, and in the sky—
even they have fallen asleep, gazed upon by the intoxicating sidelong glances of young women.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you; may it be a radiant morning. 16 [17]
O sages, even the great ones here— Vatsa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Adrikratu, Pulaha, Vasiṣṭha, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and Gārgya— even they,
when ever attached to the hips of young women, fall into perpetual sleep.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. 17 [16]
Deprived of food and clothing, devoted to the yoke of death, beset by many and various calamities, their bodies consumed like ghosts,
they are devoid of both [human] destinies; even they lie there naked and fast asleep.
O Ten-Powered One, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you; may the day break auspiciously. [18] (15)

O Protector, whatever merit has arisen for me through my devotion by proclaiming even a mere fraction of your qualities— a merit purified by the splendor of its true nature— may that, in this world, swiftly destroy all imitation.
O Daśabala, may there always be a beautiful dawn for you at daybreak. ||19||
A beautiful dawn belongs to you alone,
whose eye is opened by wisdom,
for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance.
The sun is eternally set. || 20 [21] ||
Again there is dawn, again the sun has risen, again the moon, and again the night;
likewise, death, old age, and birth occur yet once more.
The one of deluded intellect does not perceive the coming and going. || 21 [22] ||
While the world sleeps in the darkness of the night of the slumber of ignorance upon the broad bed of craving with sense-objects as its pillow,
it revolves through the fruits of good and evil deeds.
Salutations to him who is ever awake. ||22 [19]||
A beautiful dawn, a favorable star, greeted by prosperity—
this I bow to day after day. 23 [23]
At sacred fords, hundreds of herds of cows drink the water and attain satisfaction, yet it does not undergo depletion;
even so is it with the sage who is praised by the best of poets.
The treasury of virtues of this ocean of virtues is never exhausted. || 24 [20]||
Having praised the Teacher of the World, the supreme great sage,
the ocean of merit of the true Dharma,
who is free from conflict and has destroyed the darkness of passion and hatred;
With senses stilled and free from desire,
whatever extensive merit has been acquired by me— by that, may the entire world quickly [attain peace].
When the Daśabala was gladdened by the hymn at dawn, may they attain supreme faith. 25 [24]
The hymn of praise for a fair dawn is completed.
This is the work of King Śrī Harṣa.
